newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mahdi sees uprising, not military invasion of Sudan.
newsitem.headline: Mahdi sees uprising, not military invasion of Sudan.

text.p: Sudanese opposition leader Sadeq al-Mahdi said on Friday that a popular uprising was most likely to overthrow the government in Khartoum, rather than a military campaign from abroad, a coup d'etat or change from within.

Mahdi, who fled Khartoum last month and is now on the second stage of a tour to muster support for the opposition, also said he did not expect Egypt or many other of Sudan's neighbours to back opposition military activities from bases in Eritrea.
He played down the military aspect of the opposition's strategy, saying it was only one of many forms of pressure he hoped would tip the balance against the Khartoum government.

Mahdi was democratically elected prime minister of Sudan in 1989 when the present government seized power in a military coup. He is the leader of the powerful Umma Party and of the Ansar, the religious movement loyal to the 19th century Mahdi.

"I think the regime has already run out of steam," he told a news conference in Cairo. "It is incapable of resolving any of the country's internal or external problems. It is now hanging by the very feeblest of threads.
"The forces for a national uprising are all now quite mature in Sudan...The social forces that usually make for change are now in preparation for a decisive moment," he added.
"I think an uprising will come, however much the regime buys time, because there is no way the regime can stop the opposition rejecting it. This is the most probable outcome," he said.
The two previous undemocratic governments in Sudan -- those of Ibrahim Abboud in 1964 and Jaafar Nimeiri in 1985 -- have both fallen to popular uprisings from the streets of Khartoum.
Pressed for details of a meeting with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Thursday, Mahdi said only it was no surprise that what he called "victims of the regime" should think alike.

Historically Egypt has had bad relations with the Mahdist movement and it raised no objections to the military coup of 1989. But Cairo has since accused Khartoum of helping Egyptian Islamists who tried to kill Mubarak in Addis Ababa in 1995.
"I am not expecting any Egyptian military help in the realisation of the aims of the people of Sudan nor is it the only means by which we are working," Mahdi said.

"The military is one aspect of a wide spectrum of pressures that we hope will realise our aims...and it is clear that many of our neighbours will associate themselves with the non-violent alternatives," he added.

Mahdi said there was a very small chance that the National Islamic Front of Hassan al-Turabi, the Islamist movement which dominates the Khartoum government, might relinquish power voluntarily when it realised it had failed.
A military coup was also possible but the opposition could not count on one in its plans, he added.
Mahdi said he would stay about one week longer in Egypt and then take his diplomatic offensive to Saudi Arabia.
He declined to be drawn on what specific measures he wanted Sudan's neighbours to take to put pressure on Khartoum.
